nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Production carbon footprint reduction|Sustainable agriculture methods_qna_000
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How many articles were identified during the peer-reviewed and grey literature search?
nodes.answer: A total of 8 articles discussing comprehensive on-farm sustainability assessment instruments were identified.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract A rapid transformation to sustainable agricultural production systems is necessary, requiring on-farm monitoring and meas- urements of key agricultural sustainability indicators. While many assessment methods for agricultural sustainability incor - porate a three-pillar model of sustainability: environment, economic, and social, a step beyond this is required to support both human and planetary health. This review takes the position that a more nuanced, yet broader framing of agricultural sustainability is warranted, and identifies the measurement of additional pillars including health and nutrition, production, and responsible governance, plus overlooked aspects including Indigenous cultures. A peer-reviewed and grey literature search was conducted identifying articles (n = 8) discussing comprehensive, more than three-pillar, on-farm sustainability assess- ment instruments (n = 7). These seven instruments were analysed against an a priori framework of adaptability, modularity, practicality and scalability. Also explored was the usage of the broader sustainability pillars and common themes within the literature. Limited literature was found which encompassed the complexity of the requirements for measuring agricultural sustainability on-farm. A scalable and practical approach to the construction and use of on-farm agricultural sustainability assessment instruments is nascent.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Production carbon footprint reduction|Sustainable agriculture methods_qna_002
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What issue must be avoided when discussing agricultural sustainability, according to the review?
nodes.answer: The issue of agricultural sustainability must not become carbon myopic.
nodes.paragraph: This review recommends the examination of instruments in a participatory and transdis - ciplinary manner to ensure effective operationalisation, acknowledge place-based nuance, and support farmers as potential end-users. Moving forward, the application and design of sustainable agriculture assessment instruments needs to encompass the full range of externalities created by agricultural production systems to actualise sustainability. Keywords Sustainable agriculture On-farm sustainability metrics Place-based sustainability Agricultural sustainability assessment Background Many of Earth S systems are extensively impacted by mod- ern agricultural practices (Campbell et al. 2017). While there is much warranted attention placed on both the climate change aspects and carbon reduction potential of agriculture (Jaiswal and Agrawal 2020; Ozlu et al. 2022), care must be taken not to make the issue of agricultural sustainability carbon myopic (Savasta-Kennedy 2014). A key Earth sys- tem negatively impacted by agricultural practices includes drastically altered biogeochemical flows via inappropriate nutrient use, for example, nitrogen (Vira et al. 2020). Agri- culture has also contributed to massive land-use changes and biodiversity loss (Campbell et al. 2017; Gerten et al. 2020), damaging the integrity of the biosphere (Rockstr m et al.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What does the review discuss regarding agricultural sustainability evaluation methods?
nodes.answer: It discusses indicators, metrics, tools, or frameworks used to measure sustainability performance of agricultural operations.
nodes.paragraph: 2021). Monitoring and measurement of agricultural practices can support progress towards long-term sustainability and support sustainable development (Calleros-Islas 2019), while the implementation of well-designed sustainability metrics can ensure transparency and rigor within the meas- urement process (Fanzo et al. 2021). Further, this can guide accountability of key agricultural systems stakeholders and the implementation of evidence-based policy for supporting more sustainable production (B hringer and Jochem 2007; Fanzo et al. 2021). For clarity, this review discusses methods for evaluating on-farm sustainability, which may incorporate indicators, metrics, tools or frameworks used to measure sustainability performance of an agricultural operation; this measurement generally occurs across one or more sustain- ability pillars (FAO 2014). A pillar represents a domain or category of sustainability that is relevant to agriculture; each pillar consists of qualitative or quantitative indicators that are utilised to monitor or benchmark the progress in rela- tion to a sustainability target. This review will utilise the terminology Comprehensive Assessment Instrument (CAI), or instrument when referring to agricultural sustainability assessment methods. The status quo for agricultural sustainability measure- ment centres around the three-pillar model of sustainable development including economic, social, and environmental domains (James and Magee 2016; Magrini et al.

nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What types of farming methods are emphasized as necessary for sustainability?
nodes.answer: Ecologically compatible, holistic, and organic farming methods are emphasized as necessary for sustainability.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Sustainable approaches in the agricultural sector are important to addressing problems relating to food security and nutrition around the globe. To obviate these problems, it has become crucial to administer methods of farming that are ecologically compatible, holistic and organic in nature. Dutch farmers are moving towards more sustainable and circular production methods to respond to the various challenges, including biodiversity loss and climate change, whilst maintaining a viable business model. To generate further insight into circular and nature-inclusive or nature-positive agricultural business models (CNABM), we describe a conceptual framework that could help farmers, their advisers and, possibly, 162 Circular Economy and Sustainability (2025) 5:161 192 Introduction In the past decade, the importance of sustainable food systems has been receiving increasing emphasis. Sustainable approaches in the agricultural sector are of the utmost importance to addressing problems relating to food security and nutrition around the globe. To obviate these problems, it has become crucial to administer methods of farm- ing that are ecologically compatible, holistic and organic in nature [1] ]. For farmers, this entails being confronted with increasing pressures on land and concerns about the emis- sion of greenhouse gasses, ammonia and minerals in relation to climate goals, as well as water quality and animal welfare in relation to human health [1 , 2].
